title: Thinking about amrit
hookLine: taking amrit is a personal step, taken when a person feels ready
tomorrow: Simran makes a list. what exactly does amrit ask of her?

lines: A SIGN-UP SHEET. A PEN ON A STRING.
BEBE: THE PEN ISN'T GOING ANYWHERE.
cards: A sign-up sheet on a cork board, a pen on a string, three names already on it. Simran is standing in the gurdwara hallway after Sunday langar, still holding a paper plate she forgot to throw away.
The flyer says an amrit sanchar, the ceremony for taking amrit, is coming at the end of the month. The second name on the sheet is Jasleen, her friend from Gurmat camp. Simran picks up the pen.
Puts it down. Picks it up again. Behind her, a slow voice says: that pen isn't going anywhere, beti.

teach.h: AMRIT: THE STEP INTO THE KHALSA.
teach.b: Here's what Simran is looking at. Taking amrit is the step by which a Sikh joins the Khalsa, the community of initiated Sikhs.
Five initiated Sikhs prepare amrit, a sweetened water, and give it, and those who take it commit to keep the five Ks and a daily discipline.

teach.h: THE CODE: WILLING, AND OLD ENOUGH.
teach.b: The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, says who may take it: any man or woman, of any background, who is willing to keep the vows and is old enough to understand them. Notice what it doesn't set: a deadline.
No age by which you must.

teach.h: NO DEADLINE, NO LIST OF WHO'S LATE.
teach.b: No list of who's late. So how does a person know? The Granth answers with a picture, not a rule.

teach.h: ANG 1412: THE HEAD ON YOUR PALM.
teach.b: On ang 1412, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: if you long to play the game of love, come to my lane with your head on your palm. Set foot on this path, and give your head without a second thought.
Read slowly, the image isn't a dare. It's what readiness looks like from the inside: the head is already in your hand before you walk in. Nobody pushes it there.
That's why Bebe isn't rushing her.
Jasleen's name on the sheet is Jasleen's yes. It doesn't make it Simran's time. The signal isn't the sheet filling up.
It's the step starting to feel like hers.

how: Gurdwaras hold amrit sanchar ceremonies from time to time; people who wish to take amrit speak with the organizers beforehand, and the decision is their own.

o: studying the history of amrit for a school paper
planning the food for a gurdwara celebration
weighing whether you're ready to join the Khalsa

games.q: the step and its words — tap the pairs.
p: come with your head on your palm

s: Sikhs are expected to take amrit by a set age
the code sets no deadline; it asks that a person be willing and old enough to understand the vows.
the code opens amrit to any man or woman willing to keep the vows
of any background, once they're old enough to understand them.
the head-on-your-palm line is a dare to prove your courage
read slowly, it pictures readiness: the head is already in your hand before you walk in.

games.q: your cousin says his friends are all getting engaged this year, so he'd better propose too. going by today, what's the honest question?
o: is this his own yes, or just everyone else's timing?
how fast can he catch up before he's the last one?
should he wait until he's sure about absolutely everything?
games.why: Jasleen's name on the sheet was Jasleen's yes. readiness is the step feeling like yours, not the sheet filling up.

practice: Take a scrap of paper and write one sentence by hand: I'll know I'm ready for this when… It can be about any big step in your life, not only this one. Read it back once, put the pen down, and sit with the sentence.

wordCard.voice: Thinking about amrit. Weighing the step into the Khalsa, a step taken when a person is ready, not when the sheet fills up.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: amrit, nectar; the sweetened water of the Khalsa initiation.

carryVoice: Your line: when ready. The head on the palm is never pushed there. More tomorrow.
